solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Northerner initially moaning on beds in sick bay

indicators.note: what comes initially is at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
in an across clue one thing sitting on another comes after it, so this piece is written second
being in something means sitting inside it, so these pieces go within the outer word

blocks.note: cots are small beds
opening letter of moaning
SAN is short for sanatorium, a sick bay

explanation.surface: A northerner lies groaning on a bed in the infirmary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northerner' sounds vague, but in a British paper it points north of the border; sick bay abbreviates sanatorium, a common crossword stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scotsman comes from Scotland, the far north of Britain, so he is a northerner by geography.

clue.text: Fellow celeb originally idolised around mountainous state

indicators.note: what something was originally is how it began, so the word's first letter is kept

blocks.note: a co-star is a fellow celebrity in the same show
first letter of idolised
CA, circa, means around

explanation.surface: A fellow celebrity who was first idolised somewhere in a hilly country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a container signal, but here it simply supplies CA, the abbreviation of circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Costa Rica is a Central American republic whose interior is dominated by volcanic mountain ranges.

clue.text: In Times, article following first of Reith lectures

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
one thing following another comes after it, so this piece is written second
being in something means sitting inside it, so these letters go within the outer word

blocks.note: tide is an old word for time or season, as in Yuletide
first letter of Reith
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A Times piece about the Reith Lectures, the BBC's annual radio talks.
explanation.walkthrough: R then A sits inside TIDES; 'Times' is capitalised to look like the newspaper, but it means tides, as in 'time and tide'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tirades are long angry speeches, and lectures in the sense of scoldings are much the same thing.

clue.text: Meanie in firm is erratic …

indicators.note: the answer is found in the run of letters that follows, straddling the word breaks

blocks.note: the letters sit across the end of firm, all of is and the start of erratic

explanation.surface: A mean colleague in a company behaves unpredictably.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue's surface to the next one; the answer is spelt out across the end of 'firm', 'is' and 'erratic'.
explanation.definitionFit: A meanie is a stingy person, and a miser hoards money and hates spending it.

clue.text: … and not half common!

indicators.note: keeping half of a word means cutting away the other half of its letters

blocks.note: normal means ordinary or common

explanation.surface: Carrying on from the previous clue: the meanie is not even halfway common.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three letters of NORMAL survive; the dots join this clue's surface to the one before.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction nor adds a further negative, doing the same job as the phrase meaning also not.

clue.text: Reportedly observe and intimidate marine mammal

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: to see is to observe
to cow someone is to intimidate them

explanation.surface: Someone watches and then bullies a large creature of the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first part is spoken; COW is taken as a plain synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea cow is the common name for the dugong and manatee, slow plant-eating mammals of warm coastal waters.

clue.text: Bird from south currently settled on tailor’s iron

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation
now means at present
a goose is a tailor's heavy smoothing iron, named for its curved handle

explanation.surface: A bird from the south has perched on a tailor's pressing iron.
explanation.walkthrough: A tailor's goose is a real old term for the heavy iron used to press cloth, which makes the surface bird-heavy on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow goose is a white Arctic-breeding species of goose, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Article Irish left in travel complex

blocks.note: the indefinite article
IR is an abbreviation for Irish
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about an Irish person abandoned in a travel hub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' reads as abandoned, but it gives PORT, the sailor's word for the left-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: An airport is a large set of terminals and runways built for passengers setting off on journeys.

clue.text: City given prestigious award — I’m surprised!

blocks.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
aha is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed that a city has received a grand prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The Order of Merit is a very exclusive British honour given by the monarch, hence 'prestigious'.
explanation.definitionFit: Omaha is the largest urban centre in Nebraska, on the Missouri River in the United States.

clue.text: Old ruler head of school dropped in flipping grass

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top letter, so only the opening one is kept
flipping something over turns it end to end, so the letters run backwards
something dropped in lands inside another thing, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to grass is to inform, and a rat is an informer
first letter of school

explanation.surface: A former headmaster is being told off in angry language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' passes for a mild British swearword, but it reverses RAT; grass is British slang for an informer, so is rat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was an emperor of Russia before 1917, so an autocrat of the past.

clue.text: Former language bores actor when translated

indicators.note: translation turns words into a new form, so the letters are rendered in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old language that makes a performer yawn once it is put into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' fits the language theme, which disguises it as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Serbo-Croat was the official language of Yugoslavia, now usually treated as separate Serbian, Croatian and Bosnian.

clue.text: Leningrad’s unusual variety of shore bird

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters are not in their normal order

blocks.note: the city name with its S

explanation.surface: A rare type of wading bird found around the old Soviet city of Leningrad.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A sanderling is a small pale sandpiper that runs along beaches at the edge of the waves.

clue.text: Early childhood, I suspect, includes introduction to neighbours

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
to include something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: I fancy is a way of saying I suspect
first letter of neighbours

explanation.surface: Someone guesses their first years included meeting the people next door.
explanation.walkthrough: N sits inside the phrase I FANCY, splitting it after the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Infancy is the first stage of a person's life, from birth to toddlerhood.

clue.text: See about getting artist involved in examination

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
being involved in something puts you inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning see or behold
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: Look into a painter being tested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the old exclamation meaning behold, not the verb of vision, and the artist is a Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral is a spoken test, as opposed to a written paper, so it is a kind of exam.

clue.text: Sheriff’s officer spat furiously during argument

indicators.note: doing something furiously means wildly, so the letters are thrown into disorder
during means in the middle of, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a tiff is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: A sheriff's man spat angrily in the middle of a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spat' also means a quarrel, which sits nicely beside 'argument', but here it is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A tipstaff is an official who carried a metal-tipped staff and acted for a sheriff or court, like a bailiff.

clue.text: Man after a vote and a nervous affliction — that’s self-evident

indicators.note: one thing coming after another is written later, so the ordering of these pieces is set by this word

blocks.note: taken as written
X is the cross marked on a ballot paper
IOM is the Isle of Man
taken as written
a tic is a nervous twitch

explanation.surface: A man twitches nervously after voting, and it is plain to see why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is capitalised because it is the Isle of Man, a British Crown dependency; its abbreviation comes after A and X.
explanation.definitionFit: Something axiomatic is taken as an unquestioned truth, so it needs no proof and is obvious.

clue.text: Expenditure not in place

blocks.note: out is the opposite of in
to lay something is to place it

explanation.surface: Spending money that is out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place' reads as a noun but is the verb, to lay down.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlay is money laid out on something, the amount spent on a purchase or project.

clue.text: Like second coffee? Send out new aide

indicators.note: sending someone out removes them from the room, so a letter leaves the word

blocks.note: as means like
S is the abbreviation for second
instant is powdered coffee
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you would like another coffee, then sends the new helper to fetch it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coffee' stands for a kind of coffee, the powdered sort; 'Send out' then removes only the single letter that new abbreviates.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant is a helper who supports someone senior, which is what an aide does.

clue.text: Seasoned food served by girl with friend in Paris

blocks.note: Sal is a girl's name
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A waitress and her friend bring out spicy food in a Paris café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Paris' tells you to give the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a cured sausage heavily spiced with garlic and pepper, so it is a highly flavoured meat.

clue.text: Craftsman lives with terrier at first in Atlantic islands

indicators.note: what comes at first is at the very start, so only the opening letter is kept
being in a place means being inside it, so these letters go within the outer word

blocks.note: first letter of terrier
is means exists or lives
the Aran Islands lie off the west coast of Ireland

explanation.surface: A craftsman lives with his terrier on some Atlantic islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The Aran Islands lie off Galway in the west of Ireland and are famous for a style of knitwear, which suits a craftsman.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker who makes things by hand, such as a potter or weaver.

clue.text: Want son to entertain the French? That’s uncalled-for

indicators.note: a host entertains guests inside the home, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: to want is to need
S is the abbreviation for son
les is the French plural for the

explanation.surface: A parent asks whether their son wants to host French guests, then says there is no call for it.
explanation.walkthrough: NEEDS holds LES before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless describes something with no necessity or justification, the same sense as unwarranted and gratuitous.

clue.text: Hero’s lover’s name revealed in editorial

indicators.note: something revealed in a place is found inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a leader is a newspaper's editorial article
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A newspaper editorial names the man a celebrated hero loved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hero' reads as a brave man, but it is the priestess of Greek myth; LEADER is the British term for a newspaper's opinion column.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to meet his beloved Hero, and drowned in a storm.

clue.text: Assist in a B movie?

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
ET is Spielberg's film about an alien

explanation.surface: Helping out on a low-budget film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'B movie' is a single phrase in the surface, but the B stands alone and the film is ET.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to help or encourage someone, usually in wrongdoing, as in aiding and abetting.

clue.text: Runner possibly taking over party

blocks.note: a runner bean is a climbing garden vegetable
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: An athlete perhaps takes charge of a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' sounds like an athlete; the 'possibly' says it is an example, the runner bean.
explanation.definitionFit: Beano is informal British slang for a celebration or a lively knees-up.

clue.text: Month one catches girl from East dressing?

indicators.note: reading from the east means going right to left, so the letters run backwards
to catch something is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: May is a month
taken as written
Sian is a Welsh girl's name

explanation.surface: A month in which someone catches a girl from the East wearing clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressing' tempts as clothing; it is salad dressing, the definition, and the question mark flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayonnaise is a thick cold sauce of egg yolk and oil, used as a salad dressing.

clue.text: Musical work: I must be inspired holy writ?

indicators.note: to be inspired is to be breathed in, so one piece is taken inside the other

blocks.note: NT is the New Testament
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A composer insists that a piece of music must be divinely inspired, like scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inspired' is used literally, breathed in, and I becomes ONE, not the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a composition for nine players or singers, so it is a piece of music.

clue.text: Wind instrument delivered — advantage husband accepted

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so these letters are held inside the outer word

blocks.note: a baby delivered is born
an asset is an advantage
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A wind instrument was delivered, and a husband got the benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivered' reads as a courier's word, but it is the birth sense; the advantage and the husband go into it together as one chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The basset horn is a tenor member of the clarinet family, beloved of Mozart, and is blown like any woodwind.

clue.text: Work laboriously, lacking time to get fuel

indicators.note: something lacking a part is without it, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: to toil is to work hard
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone slogs away without a break to earn money for fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: The T comes off the front of TOIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil is burnt in engines and boilers as an energy source, which is exactly what fuel means.

clue.text: Setback for old archbishop’s double

indicators.note: a setback sends things back the way they came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: William Laud was Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I

explanation.surface: A reversal of fortune for a former archbishop's lookalike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' reads as a lookalike noun, but it is the adjective meaning twofold.
explanation.definitionFit: Dual means consisting of two parts, as in dual carriageway, the adjectival sense of twofold.

clue.text: Senior officer given bill covering case of gin and brandy

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters are kept
covering something means going around it, so the joined pieces enclose the others

blocks.note: CO is a commanding officer
AC is short for account, a bill
outer letters of gin

explanation.surface: A senior officer is handed a bill for a crate of gin and some brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: The officer and the bill are joined first, and that pair then wraps round the outside letters of the spirit, so the bill comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a fine grape spirit made in the Cognac region of France, and is the best-known brandy.

clue.text: Educated Liberal fuming about note

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
fuming means very angry
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A well-schooled Liberal politician is seething about a memo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' suggests a message, but it is a musical note from do-re-mi.
explanation.definitionFit: Literate means able to read and write, and more broadly well read and cultured.
